en.title: Fine and Applied Arts: the whole course
en.short: What fine and applied arts covers, how art degrees are organised, the studio areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: Fine and Applied Arts is the study and practice of making images and objects, and of understanding them in history and society. Fine art is work made mainly for expression, contemplation or exhibition, such as drawing, painting, sculpture and printmaking. Applied arts are made for a use or a client, such as graphic design, textiles, ceramics and illustration. The two are taught together because both depend on drawing, design, materials and judgement. The course also teaches art history, criticism, curatorship and professional practice, so graduates can work as artists, designers, teachers, gallery staff, researchers or studio managers. It is not only hand skill. It is visual thinking backed by reading, writing and research.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text: Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, universities commonly offer a four-year bachelor’s degree with titles such as BA Fine and Applied Arts; some institutions use BFA or similar titles. Polytechnics commonly offer ND and HND awards, often two years each, with studio work and industrial attachment. The NUC guides university programmes and the NBTE guides polytechnic programmes. In the United Kingdom, a bachelor’s degree is commonly three years; in the United States it is commonly four. Master’s awards take one to two years. Admission often includes a portfolio or practical test. First-year work usually covers drawing, design, colour, materials and art history. Later years add studio specialisms, theory, research and a final project or exhibition. Confirm duration, award title and entry rules with your department.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The introductory stage builds visual language. You study drawing from observation, the elements and principles of design, colour theory, two-dimensional composition and three-dimensional form and space. You also learn materials, tools and workshop safety, then art history methods and a world survey to the early modern period. African art traditions and visual analysis teach you to read form, iconography (subject matter and symbols) and context.

The core stage is studio-based. Painting, sculpture, printmaking, ceramics, textiles, graphic design, typography, illustration, photography and digital media each introduce a medium, its tools and its workflow. Alongside them you study modern and contemporary art history, criticism and curatorship, the work of selecting, caring for and interpreting collections, museum and gallery studies, art education and community practice, professional practice and research methods. The course usually ends with a final project and exhibition.

At master’s level, work becomes more independent. You study advanced art theory and aesthetics, research methods for a dissertation, contemporary African art and globalisation, and advanced studio practice with an exhibition.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Draw regularly from life, not only from photographs. Short daily studies improve observation faster than occasional long pieces. For each medium, learn the basic process in order: prepare the surface or material, control the tool, finish and clean up. Read art history with images open. For each work, identify subject, form, material, context and likely purpose. Compare works rather than memorising isolated dates.

Use feedback. Write down what a lecturer or technician says, then make one change in the next work. Keep a sketchbook, a process file and a simple inventory of finished work. Learn the vocabulary of design and criticism so you can explain decisions. Workshop safety is part of the subject: learn the rules for blades, presses, kilns, solvents, dust, electrical tools and ventilation before you use them. Ask for supervision when unsure.

For research, use library databases and official museum or gallery sources, and cite them. Check current exhibition and competition deadlines from the organiser, not from old posts.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
A common mistake is treating fine art as only feeling and applied art as only software. Both need observation, composition and clear thinking. Another is copying a style without understanding its materials or context. Students also neglect safety rules, leave cleanup to others, or work without documenting stages.

In writing, common faults are describing a work without evidence, using vague praise such as beautiful, and presenting one country’s art history as universal. Name the culture, period and place. In professional practice, do not invent prices, awards or exhibition records. In research, do not claim that a small sample proves a broad conclusion. Finally, do not leave the final project and exhibition to the last weeks. Plan production, framing, labelling and installation early.

keyPoints: Fine and Applied Arts combines studio making with art history, criticism and professional practice.
Award titles and course length differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Drawing, design and colour are the foundation for every later studio medium.
Workshop safety and clean working habits are part of the course, not optional extras.
Art history and visual analysis require evidence about form, material, context and place.
Plan the final project and exhibition early, and document your work as you go.

en.title: Drawing foundations: observation and visual language
en.short: Observing still life and the figure through line, tone, proportion, perspective and composition.

sections.heading: Observation and line
sections.text: Observational drawing begins with looking, not guessing. Sit so you can see the subject, then compare angles, lengths and spaces. Line can describe an edge, a contour or movement. Contour drawing follows the edge slowly; gesture drawing captures the whole pose in quick, loose marks. A sketchbook is a working record, not a gallery: date pages, note the light and try many small studies. Keep the wrist free and draw from the shoulder for long lines.

sections.heading: Tone and proportion
sections.text: Tone means light and dark. Squint to simplify values into light, middle and dark, then build layers from light to dark. Proportion is the size relationship between parts. Measure by holding a pencil at arm’s length, closing one eye, and marking a length with your thumb; compare that unit with other parts. For example, if a bottle measures 12 cm high and 4 cm wide on your pencil, its height-to-width ratio is 12 ÷ 4 = 3:1, so draw it three times as tall as wide. For the figure, many traditions use about seven to eight head lengths for a standing adult, but real bodies vary, so measure your model.

sections.heading: Perspective and composition
sections.text: Perspective makes flat drawings suggest depth. In one-point perspective, parallel lines receding from the viewer meet at a vanishing point on the horizon. Overlap, size change and placement also show depth. Composition arranges the drawing on the page: choose a clear focal point, leave breathing space, and avoid cutting joints awkwardly in a figure. A viewfinder, a card with a rectangular hole, helps you frame the subject before drawing.

sections.heading: Sketchbook and media safety
sections.text: Use graphite, charcoal, conté or ink according to the effect you want. Keep charcoal and pastel dust away from your face; do not blow it. Work in a ventilated room when using fixative and follow the label. Wash hands after handling media, keep ink away from your mouth, and store sharp tools safely. Regular short sketchbook sessions build visual memory better than occasional long ones.

keyPoints: Observational drawing starts with sustained looking and comparing angles, lengths and spaces.
Line can be contour, following an edge, or gesture, capturing the whole pose quickly.
Tone is organised into light, middle and dark values before detail.
Proportion compares lengths; a 12 cm high and 4 cm wide object gives 12 ÷ 4 = 3:1.
In one-point perspective, receding parallel lines meet at a vanishing point on the horizon.
Use drawing media in a ventilated space, avoid inhaling dust, and follow fixative labels.

en.title: Elements and principles of design: the visual vocabulary
en.short: The visual elements and organising principles used to describe and make two- and three-dimensional art.

sections.heading: Elements in two dimensions
sections.text: The elements are the basic visual qualities an artist uses. A line is a mark with length and direction, made by a moving point. A shape is a flat enclosed area, such as a circle or a letter. Value is the lightness or darkness of a tone. Texture is the surface quality, real or suggested. Colour is what we see when light is reflected from a surface. Space is the area around, between or inside shapes; in a flat picture, overlapping and size can suggest depth.

sections.heading: Form and three dimensions
sections.text: Form is a three-dimensional mass with height, width and depth, such as a pot or a carved figure. In three dimensions, space is the volume a form occupies and the room around it. Texture may be actual, as in rough clay, or visual. A pot can be described by its form, its proportion and the negative space inside its opening. A poster can be described by its lines, shapes, values and colours.

sections.heading: Principles of organisation
sections.text: Principles are ways of arranging elements. Balance distributes visual weight; it may be symmetrical or asymmetrical. Rhythm is repeated or varied elements that create movement. Proportion compares sizes. Emphasis makes one part dominant. Unity makes a work feel whole, while variety supplies difference and interest. These principles work together: too much unity can be dull, too much variety chaotic.

sections.heading: Using the terms
sections.text: To describe a work, name the elements you see and the principles that organise them. In a campus exhibition poster, a repeated diagonal line may create rhythm, a large title shape may give emphasis, and a small dark shape on the opposite side may balance it. In a clay pot, a wide body and narrow neck set up proportion, and the curved surface catches light to create value. The same vocabulary works for drawing, design, sculpture and craft.

keyPoints: Elements are the basic visual qualities: line, shape, form, value, texture, colour and space.
Principles are ways of arranging elements: balance, rhythm, proportion, emphasis, unity and variety.
Shape is flat; form has volume and exists in three dimensions.
Balance distributes visual weight, and it can be symmetrical or asymmetrical.
Unity and variety must be held in tension so a composition is coherent but not dull.
Use the same vocabulary to describe a poster, a pot or a carving.

en.title: Colour theory and practice: hue, value and mixing
en.short: Hue, value, chroma, colour wheels, pigment mixing, contrast, schemes and cultural meaning.

sections.heading: Three dimensions
sections.text: Colour has three dimensions. Hue is the family name, such as red or blue. Value is lightness or darkness. Chroma, or saturation, is strength or purity. A tint is lightened with white, a shade darkened with black, and a tone softened with grey. These words let you describe a colour precisely.

sections.heading: Wheels and mixing
sections.text: The traditional artist’s colour wheel uses red, yellow and blue as primaries, with orange, green and violet as secondaries. It is a teaching model, not a physical law. Pigment mixing is subtractive: pigments absorb some light and reflect the rest. Printing uses cyan, magenta and yellow; light uses red, green and blue. Mixing two primaries makes a secondary. Complementary colours, opposite on the wheel, dull each other. Exercise: mix a secondary, then add a little of the third primary and watch it dull. For a five-step value scale use 100% pigment, 3 parts pigment to 1 part white, 1 to 1, 1 part pigment to 3 parts white, and near white. Label each swatch.

sections.heading: Contrast and schemes
sections.text: Warm colours such as red, orange and yellow tend to advance; cool colours such as blue and green tend to recede. The effect is relative. Schemes include monochromatic (one hue with value and chroma changes), analogous (neighbours), complementary (opposites), split-complementary (a hue plus the neighbours of its opposite) and triadic (three evenly spaced hues). Test schemes in small swatches.

sections.heading: Perception and culture
sections.text: Perception is active. Simultaneous contrast makes a colour look different against another background; afterimages and colour constancy show the eye and brain adjust. Colour blindness affects hue discrimination, so do not rely on colour alone. Cultural meanings vary: white can suggest mourning or celebration; red can signal danger, luck or ceremony. In Nigeria the flag’s green and white are official symbols, but everyday meanings depend on community and context. Practical work: keep labelled swatches and note lighting, proportions and drying shifts.

keyPoints: Hue is the colour family; value is lightness; chroma is saturation or purity.
A tint adds white, a shade adds black and a tone adds grey.
Pigment mixing is subtractive; light mixing is additive, so primaries differ by system.
Complementary colours sit opposite on the wheel and dull each other when mixed.
Warm colours tend to advance and cool colours recede, but the effect is relative.
Common schemes are monochromatic, analogous, complementary, split-complementary and triadic.

en.title: Two-dimensional design and composition
en.short: Framing, layout, positive and negative space, pattern, repetition, scale and visual hierarchy on flat surfaces.

sections.heading: Frame and layout
sections.text:
Two-dimensional design arranges shapes and images on a flat surface. The frame is the edge of that surface: paper, canvas or screen. Framing decides what is included or cut off. A wide margin can feel calm; a shape touching the edge can create tension.

Layout is the planned position of parts inside the frame. Start with a simple grid, then place the largest or most important element first. In a poster, the eye should find the main message before the details.

sections.heading: Space and pattern
sections.text:
Positive space is occupied by shapes or letters; negative space is the empty area around and between them. Negative space is active: it separates forms and gives them room. Pattern is a repeated motif. Repetition is the repeated use of a shape, line or interval. Repetition can create rhythm, but exact repetition may look static; changing size or spacing adds variety.

In surface design, a motif is repeated in a grid, or with rows shifted by half a motif. The repeat must join at the edges so the design tiles without a visible seam.

sections.heading: Scale and hierarchy
sections.text:
Scale is the size of an element compared with others or with the frame. Visual hierarchy is the order in which the eye notices things. Hierarchy is built by size, contrast, placement and isolation. A large headline at the top, a smaller image and small body text give a clear order.

If every element is large or dark, nothing stands out. Check hierarchy by squinting: the main shape should remain clear.

sections.heading: Three exercises
sections.text:
Collage: cut ten paper shapes and arrange them in a 20 cm × 30 cm frame. Make one version with equal spacing and one with varied spacing; compare the negative space. Poster layout: on A4 paper, place a title, one image and three lines of text. Use a 3 × 4 grid and keep one margin wider.

Surface design: draw a 5 cm square motif, repeat it four times in a 10 cm square, and check that the edges match.

keyPoints: The frame sets the boundary of a flat design and framing decides what is included or cut off.
Layout is the planned position of elements; a grid helps place the main element first.
Positive space holds shapes or letters, while negative space is the active empty area around them.
Pattern repeats a motif; repetition creates rhythm, and varied size or spacing prevents stiffness.
Scale compares sizes, and visual hierarchy is the order in which the eye notices elements.
Collage, poster layout and surface repeat exercises build control of the flat field.

en.title: Three-dimensional design: form and space
en.short: Volume, mass, structure, scale, balance and space, with maquettes, joining and safe model making.

sections.heading: Volume and mass
sections.text: A three-dimensional (3D) object has height, width and depth. Volume is the amount of space it encloses or occupies. Mass is the visual and physical sense of weight and solidity. A hollow box and a solid block can have the same outline but different mass. Form is the shape and structure of the object; space is the air around and inside it. Positive space is occupied by the object, negative space is the gap it leaves.

sections.heading: Structure and scale
sections.text: Structure is how parts support one another and carry loads. A simple model must stand without collapsing. Scale is the ratio between model and real object. In a 1:10 maquette, 1 cm stands for 10 cm, so a 2 m table becomes 20 cm long. A maquette is a small trial model. It tests form, proportion and structure before full size work. Keep the same proportions when changing scale.

sections.heading: Balance and space
sections.text: Balance is the distribution of visual weight. A symmetrical form has equal weight on both sides of an axis. Asymmetrical balance uses different shapes or positions to feel stable. A tall form with a small base may look top-heavy. Spatial relationships describe how forms sit in relation to each other and to the viewer: near or far, overlapping or separate, enclosing or open. Walk around a model to check it from several sides.

sections.heading: Models, joining and safety
sections.text: For a simple maquette, choose card, foam board, balsa wood or wire. Plan the joins. A butt joint meets edge to edge and needs glue. A lap joint overlaps two pieces. A slot joint cuts notches so parts lock without glue. A pin or dowel joint uses a rod. Score card before folding. Cut on a cutting mat, away from your body, with a sharp blade and a metal rule. Keep fingers behind the blade. Wear eye protection when drilling or sanding, work in a well-ventilated space, and follow workshop rules for glues and dust. Ask a technician before using an unfamiliar tool.

keyPoints: Volume is the space a form occupies or encloses; mass is its sense of weight and solidity.
Structure is how parts support each other and carry loads.
Scale compares model to real object: a 1:10 model is one tenth of real size.
Balance distributes visual weight; spatial relationships describe how forms relate to each other and the viewer.
A maquette is a small trial model used to test form, proportion and structure.
Use sharp tools on a cutting mat, cut away from the body, and follow workshop safety rules.

en.title: Materials, tools and workshop safety
en.short: Properties and handling of paper, clay, wood, metal, textile, paint and digital tools, plus safety and waste.

sections.heading: Materials and properties
sections.text: Art materials are chosen for how they behave, not only how they look. Paper is graded by weight in grams per square metre (gsm) and by grain, the direction its fibres lie. A sheet 0.5 m × 0.7 m of 120 gsm paper weighs 0.5 × 0.7 × 120 = 42 g. Clay is plastic when damp, then shrinks as it dries and fires. Wood has grain and moves with moisture. Metal work-hardens when hammered. Textiles differ by fibre and weave. Paint is pigment in a binder, thinned by a solvent. Digital tools are hardware and software: tablet, stylus, scanner, printer.

sections.heading: Tools and care
sections.text: Keep cutting tools sharp: a blunt blade needs more force and slips. Clean brushes with the right solvent, shape the bristles, and dry them head down; never leave them standing in water. Wipe and lightly oil metal tools. Store blades, gouges and needles in a rack or roll, not loose in a drawer. Digital equipment needs surge protection and careful handling of cables and ports.

sections.heading: Safety in the workshop
sections.text: Two hazards dominate: dust and solvent vapour. Silica dust from dry clay and sawdust from wood harm the lungs, so sand and saw with extraction or a fitted mask. Solvents and spray paints give off vapour: ventilate the room, keep ignition sources away, and store liquids in closed, labelled metal cabinets. Wear goggles when mixing or grinding, and gloves with dyes and mordants, the metal salts that fix dye. Know where the first aid kit and fire extinguisher are. Rules differ by country and institution, so check your school’s code.

sections.heading: Storage and waste
sections.text: Label every container. Store heavy items low, and keep solvents away from oxidisers, chemicals that feed fires. Never pour solvents, paint or plaster water down a sink: plaster sets and blocks drains, and solvents pollute water. Use labelled waste containers, and put sharps in a rigid box. Rags soaked in oil or solvent can self-ignite, so keep them in a closed metal bin.

keyPoints: Materials are chosen for how they behave: paper by gsm and grain, clay by plasticity and shrinkage, paint by binder and solvent.
A sheet’s weight in grams equals its area in square metres multiplied by its gsm figure.
Sharp tools are safer than blunt ones; clean, dry and store them properly.
Dust and solvent vapour are the main workshop hazards, so ventilate and wear the right protection.
Never pour solvents, paint or plaster water down a sink; use labelled waste containers.
Safety rules vary by country and institution, so check your school’s own code.

en.title: Art history methods and world survey to the early modern period
en.short: Dating, attribution, description and context from prehistory to the early modern period.

sections.heading: Methods and evidence
sections.text: Art historians ask what a work is, when and where it was made, who made it and why. Dating uses style, inscriptions, documents and scientific tests: radiocarbon for organic matter, dendrochronology for wood, thermoluminescence for fired clay. Attribution proposes an artist, workshop or region. It draws on connoisseurship, close comparison with secure works, signatures, contracts, workshop records and technical imaging. Provenance is ownership history. These are arguments that can be revised.

sections.heading: Formal and contextual
sections.text: Formal analysis describes the visible object: line, shape, colour, light, composition, scale, material and technique. Contextual analysis asks about function, patron, audience, religion, politics, workshop and trade. A patron commissions and usually pays for a work. Take the Parthenon frieze in Athens, part of a temple built 447 to 432 BCE. Formally, it shows low relief, repeating figures and ideal bodies. Contextually, it belongs to a temple of Athena and likely shows the Panathenaic procession, within a civic building programme associated with Pericles.

sections.heading: Survey examples
sections.text: Prehistoric Lascaux cave paintings in France use mineral pigments and charcoal on limestone; their purpose is uncertain. The Egyptian Palette of Narmer, about 3100 BCE, is a siltstone ceremonial object often linked to royal power and unification. Roman concrete allowed the Pantheon’s dome, rebuilt under Hadrian in the second century CE. The Book of Kells, an Insular (Ireland and Britain) gospel book of about 800 CE, is painted on vellum in a monastery. The Ghent Altarpiece, completed in 1432, is oil on panel, commissioned by Jodocus Vijd for a chapel in Ghent.

sections.heading: Periods and caution
sections.text: Labels such as prehistoric, ancient, classical, medieval and early modern are useful but rough. They vary by region and scholar; early modern art history often means about 1400 to 1800. Materials and patronage affect what survives: stone and metal last better than wood or cloth, and wealthy patrons leave more records. Check dates, attributions and terms against a current museum catalogue or scholarly source.

keyPoints: Art historians date works using style, inscriptions, documents and scientific tests such as radiocarbon and dendrochronology.
Attribution proposes an artist or workshop using connoisseurship, records and technical study, and it can be revised.
Formal analysis describes visual elements; contextual analysis explains function, patron, audience and setting.
Patronage shapes a work’s subject, size and materials.
Period labels vary by region and scholar, so check dates and terms against current sources.
Selected examples from Lascaux to the Ghent Altarpiece show changes in materials and commissioning.

en.title: African art traditions: form, function and context
en.short: Regional forms, function, patronage, materials, style, and debates on collecting and repatriation.

sections.heading: Function and patronage
sections.text:
African art is rarely made only to be looked at. A mask belongs to a costume danced with music; a vessel pours palm wine; a cloth marks a funeral. Function shapes form: a head mask must be light and balanced.

Patronage is who pays for and controls the work: royal courts, shrines, age grades, title societies, families. Guilds trained artists, usually anonymous to history, though some names survive, such as the Yoruba carver Olowe of Ise.

sections.heading: Regional forms
sections.text:
Forms vary by region and period. Sculpture: Nok terracotta figures from central Nigeria (dates debated); naturalistic brass and terracotta heads from Ife; brass heads and plaques from Benin, made for the Edo court.

Textiles: Asante kente in Ghana, woven in narrow strips; Bamana bogolan mud cloth in Mali; Kuba raffia cut-pile cloth in the DRC. Architecture: the mud-brick Great Mosque of Djenné, Mali, replastered yearly; dry-stone walls at Great Zimbabwe; rock-hewn churches at Lalibela, Ethiopia. Body arts include beadwork and scarification; performance includes masquerade.

sections.heading: Style and material
sections.text: Style is a recognisable pattern of handling form: proportion, rhythm, surface. It changes with material; wood, forged iron and clay each demand different handling. Scholars reject terms like 'primitive' or 'tribal style' because they flatten many traditions into one and repeat colonial assumptions. The idea of one fixed style per ethnic group is also criticised: artists move, trade and innovate.

sections.heading: Collecting and return
sections.text:
Most museum collections of African art were built during colonial rule. Objects were bought, given or taken by force; the Benin works looted by a British expedition in 1897 are the clearest case. Debates now concern provenance (an object’s ownership history), display, and repatriation, the return of objects to their country of origin.

Museums argue they hold world heritage and care for it; claimants argue that removal stripped objects of context. France has returned works to the Republic of Benin, and Germany has transferred ownership of Benin bronzes to Nigeria; check current news, as agreements continue.

keyPoints: Function, use and patronage shape the form of African objects as much as appearance does.
Key traditions include Nok and Ife sculpture, Benin court brass, Asante kente, Djenné mosque architecture and masquerade.
Style is regional and changing, not fixed to an ethnic group; terms like 'primitive' and 'tribal' are rejected by scholars.
Masks and body arts are worn and performed, so a museum display shows only part of the work.
Provenance is an object’s ownership history; repatriation is the return of objects to their country of origin.
The Benin works looted in 1897 are the central case in current return debates.

en.title: Visual analysis: form, iconography and context
en.short: How to describe form, read subject and iconography, use basic semiotics, and relate art to context.

sections.heading: Formal description
sections.text: Begin with what you can see. Record medium, support (the surface, such as canvas or wood), size, condition and display. Then describe composition: how shapes, lines, colours, tones, textures and space are arranged. Note scale, balance, rhythm, focal point, light and surface marks such as brushwork or chisel cuts. Use neutral words first: “a dark red rectangle at the centre”, not “a sad red”. Formal description is the evidence base for later claims.

sections.heading: Subject and iconography
sections.text: Subject matter is what is shown: people, objects, landscape, pattern or nothing recognisable. Iconography is the study of recurring motifs and their conventional meanings. An attribute, such as a key or a staff, may identify a figure. In a hypothetical example, a carved wooden door panel in a Nigerian town museum shows a bird above a calabash. Formally it is a vertical relief with strong diagonal lines. Iconographically the bird may signal a messenger and the calabash hospitality, but check local sources; meanings vary. Do not assume every motif is a symbol.

sections.heading: Semiotics and context
sections.text: Semiotics studies signs. A sign has a signifier (the visible mark) and a signified (the idea). Peirce distinguished icon (resembles), index (points to or is caused by) and symbol (conventional). Barthes separated denotation, the literal level, from connotation, cultural associations. Context asks who made the work, for which patron (commissioner or funder), audience and setting, and how it was used or displayed. A mask in a shrine and the same mask in a museum frame carry different meanings.

sections.heading: Description, interpretation, evaluation
sections.text: Keep three questions apart. Description asks what is there. Interpretation asks what it means in its context. Evaluation asks whether it succeeds, and by which criteria: skill, function, originality, emotional force. A judgement without description and context is weak. State your evidence and allow other readings.

keyPoints: Formal description records visible evidence: medium, composition, colour, texture, scale and surface.
Iconography identifies subject matter and conventional motifs, checked against cultural sources.
Semiotics analyses signs through signifier and signified, icon, index and symbol.
Context includes maker, patron, audience, function, setting and later display.
Description, interpretation and evaluation are separate questions and should not be confused.
Support interpretations with visible evidence and contextual sources, and acknowledge uncertainty.

en.title: Painting studio: media, supports and composition
en.short: Oil, acrylic, watercolour and gouache; supports, grounds, layering, brushwork, colour mixing and composition.

sections.heading: Supports and grounds
sections.text: A support is the surface that carries paint: stretched canvas, wooden panel, board or paper. A ground is a prepared layer between support and paint. It seals the support and gives paint a consistent surface. Oil paint on canvas needs size, a glue seal, then primer, an undercoat, because oil can weaken the fibres. Acrylic can go on many supports but still benefits from priming. Watercolour and gouache need sized paper. Test new supports with a small sample first.

sections.heading: Media and layering
sections.text: Oil paint dries slowly, blends well and allows thick impasto, meaning raised paint. Acrylic dries fast, can be thinned with water and used in thin glazes, meaning transparent layers. Watercolour is transparent and flows in washes; gouache is opaque watercolour and can be reworked. Layering means building paint in stages. In oil, follow fat over lean: each later layer should contain more oil or less solvent than the one below, so it dries without cracking. Build acrylic layers quickly, but avoid overworking.

sections.heading: Brushwork and colour
sections.text: Brushwork is the visible handling of paint: broad blocking-in, or laying main shapes, dry brush and fine detail. Match the brush to the mark: a flat for blocks, a round for lines, a soft brush for edges. Pigment mixing is subtractive: added pigments absorb light, so more pigments usually dull colour. Test mixed colour on a swatch first. For example, mix ultramarine blue with burnt sienna to make a neutral dark, then add white to lighten it or black to darken it.

sections.heading: Composition and critique
sections.text: Composition arranges shapes, tones and edges in the frame. From observation, use a frame and small sketches to test the main light and dark shapes and focal point before painting. From imagination, gather studies, memory and reference images, then simplify them into a clear structure. Studio exercises can limit palette or time to force decisions. In group critique, describe what you see, ask what the painter intended and suggest one change. Keep notes and test feedback next study.

keyPoints: A support carries paint; a ground seals it and gives a consistent surface.
Oil, acrylic, watercolour and gouache differ in drying, transparency and reworkability.
Build layers deliberately; in oil follow fat over lean to reduce cracking.
Brushwork and pigment mixing should be tested on a swatch before the final surface.
Composition can be developed from observation with a frame and sketches, or from imagination with studies and simplification.
Group critique works best when comments describe, question intention and suggest one testable change.

en.title: Sculpture studio: modelling, carving, casting and construction
en.short: Covers sculpture methods in clay, plaster, wood, metal and mixed media, plus armature, scale, site and safety.

sections.heading: Methods and materials
sections.text:
The main sculpture methods are modelling, carving, casting and construction. Modelling and construction are additive; carving is subtractive; casting replaces one material with another. Modelling builds up soft material such as clay or wax. Carving removes material from wood or stone. Casting pours liquid material, often plaster or molten metal, into a mould taken from a model. Construction joins separate parts by welding, bolting, tying or gluing. Mixed media combines these approaches.

Each method has its own logic. Clay records touch, carving resists it, casting can repeat a form, and construction thinks through joints and structure.

sections.heading: Armature and scale
sections.text:
An armature is an internal frame that supports soft material and keeps a figure upright. A maquette is a small model used to test pose, proportion and cost. Scale changes weight, thickness and structural risk. A 30 cm maquette enlarged four times becomes 30 × 4 = 120 cm, or 1.2 m.

Check the arithmetic and the structure before enlarging. The ratio is 120 ÷ 30 = 4, or 1:4. Weight does not scale by the same ratio, so supports must be redesigned.

sections.heading: Site and surface
sections.text:
Site-specific work is made for one place. Outdoor sculpture must consider weather, foundations, public safety, viewpoint, lighting and maintenance. Surface is not decoration only: texture, patina, paint and sealant change how form catches light and how it ages. Patina is a surface layer on metal, often valued for colour and protection.

Test finishes on samples before applying them to the whole work. Record the materials and finishes used, because future conservation depends on that information.

sections.heading: Safe workshop
sections.text:
Safe practice begins with a risk assessment. Dust from stone, wood, clay and plaster can harm lungs; clay and stone dust may contain silica. Use dust extraction, wet methods, ventilation and suitable respiratory protection. Solvents need ventilation. Welding, molten metal and heavy lifting need trained supervision and proper equipment.

Rules differ by country and institution, so check current local regulations and workshop instructions before starting.

keyPoints: Modelling is additive, carving is subtractive, casting uses a mould, and construction joins parts.
An armature supports soft material; a maquette tests a form before enlargement.
Scale changes weight and structure, not only size: a 30 cm maquette at four times becomes 1.2 m.
Site-specific sculpture must answer weather, foundations, public safety, viewpoint and maintenance.
Surface finish changes light, touch and ageing, and should be tested and recorded.
Safe practice controls dust, silica, solvents, molten metal, welding fumes and heavy lifting, and follows local rules.

en.title: Printmaking studio: relief, intaglio, lithography and screen
en.short: Relief, intaglio, lithography and screen printing, with matrices, registration, proofs, editions, paper and safety.

sections.heading: Four processes
sections.text: Printmaking transfers an image from a matrix, the block, plate, stone or screen that carries it, to paper. In relief printing the image stands raised; the cutter removes non-image areas, ink is rolled on the surface, and pressure prints it. Woodcut and linocut are common. In intaglio the image is cut or etched below the plate surface; ink sits in the lines, the surface is wiped, and high pressure pulls paper into them. Lithography is planographic: image and non-image share one plane, and grease drawing, water and oil ink separate. Screen printing forces ink through open mesh with a squeegee; a stencil blocks the rest.

sections.heading: Matrix and registration
sections.text: Matrix preparation follows the process. Relief needs a flat block and sharp tools. Intaglio plates need bevelled edges, an acid-resist ground for etching, and careful acid use. Litho stones are grained and kept damp; screens need tension, emulsion and correct exposure. Registration keeps layers aligned: use marks, tabs or pins, and place paper consistently. For screen, set off-contact, the small gap between screen and paper, so the mesh snaps back.

sections.heading: Proofs and editions
sections.text: Proofing tests the image before the edition. A trial proof shows faults; a state proof records a stage; a printer’s proof goes to the printer who pulled the edition. Editioning is the signed run from one matrix. Number each print, for example 3/20, and keep artist’s proofs separate. In common practice, artist’s proofs are about a tenth of the edition, so an edition of 20 might have 2 artist’s proofs, giving 22 impressions in all, but the edition number stays 20. Destroy or mark spoiled prints so they cannot enter the edition.

sections.heading: Paper and safety
sections.text: Use printmaking paper that accepts ink and repeated pressure. Tear it against a straight edge to keep a deckle edge, the soft untrimmed edge, dampen intaglio paper evenly, and store prints flat, interleaved and dry. In the workshop, solvents, acids, inks, dust and screen chemicals can harm skin, eyes and lungs. Use ventilation, gloves, eye protection and safety data sheets; never eat in the studio; label containers; dispose of waste through the approved route. Check local rules.

keyPoints: Relief prints from raised areas; intaglio prints from incised lines; lithography relies on grease and water on one plane; screen printing pushes ink through open mesh.
Matrix preparation must match the process, for example sharp tools for relief, bevelled plates and controlled acid for intaglio, grained stones for lithography, and correctly exposed screens.
Registration aligns paper and matrix consistently, using marks, tabs or pins; screen printing also needs correct off-contact.
Proofing tests the image before editioning; trial proofs, state proofs and printer’s proofs have different purposes.
An edition is the signed run from one matrix; number prints as 3/20, keep artist’s proofs separate, and destroy or mark spoiled prints.
Workshop safety requires ventilation, gloves, eye protection, safety data sheets, labelling and approved waste disposal, with local rules checked.

en.title: Ceramics studio: clay, forming, firing and glazing
en.short: Clay bodies, handbuilding, throwing, joining, drying, decoration, bisque and glaze firing, kiln safety.

sections.heading: Clay bodies
sections.text:
Clay is weathered rock, mainly clay minerals, that becomes plastic when wet and hard when fired. A clay body is a mixed recipe, not one material. Earthenware matures at low temperature and stays porous unless glazed. Stoneware is denser and vitrifies, meaning it becomes glass-like and non-porous. Porcelain is white, translucent and difficult to throw. Adding grog, which is crushed pre-fired clay, reduces shrinkage and opens the body. Test any body before using it for a set.

Plasticity means the clay can be shaped without cracking. Shrinkage is the loss of size as water leaves and as the body densifies in the fire.

sections.heading: Handbuilding and throwing
sections.text:
Handbuilding uses pinching, coiling and slab building. Coils are joined with slip, a clay-and-water slurry, onto a scored surface, meaning scratched, so the parts key together. Wheel throwing centres a lump on a spinning head, opens it, pulls up walls and shapes the rim.

Walls must be even, because thick and thin parts dry and shrink at different rates and crack. Leather-hard is the stage when clay is firm enough to trim and join without collapsing.

sections.heading: Drying and surfaces
sections.text: Water leaves clay in two stages: shrinkage water between the particles, then pore water. Dry slowly under loose plastic so the whole piece loses water evenly. Surface decoration includes slip trailing, sgraffito (scratching through slip to show the body beneath), incising, stamping and texturing. Glaze is a later glassy coating, not a substitute for surface design.

sections.heading: Firing, glazes and safety
sections.text: Bisque firing hardens raw work, usually slowly, to drive off water and burn out organic matter. Glaze firing follows, usually at a higher temperature, and melts the glaze onto the body. Load the kiln with supported shelves, work clear of the elements, and space for air to move. Glaze recipes are given as percentages by weight. Scaling a 100 g batch of feldspar 40, silica 30, whiting 20 and kaolin 10 to 500 g gives 200, 150, 100 and 50 g. Ventilate the kiln area, control dust, wear protection, and never open a hot kiln.

keyPoints: A clay body is a recipe; earthenware, stoneware and porcelain mature differently.
Score and slip joints so handbuilt parts hold.
Even walls and slow drying prevent cracks.
Bisque firing hardens work; glaze firing melts the glaze onto it.
Glaze recipes are percentages by weight and scale by simple multiplication.
Kiln safety means ventilation, dust control and never opening a hot kiln.

en.title: Textiles studio: fibre, construction, dye and surface design
en.short: Fibre identification, yarn, weaving, dyeing, printing, pattern repeat, fastness and sustainability.

sections.heading: Fibres and yarns
sections.text:
Fibres are natural (cotton and linen from plants; wool and silk from animals) or manufactured, either regenerated from cellulose (viscose) or synthetic (polyester). The burn test is a rough bench check: cotton smells of burnt paper and leaves soft grey ash, wool of burnt hair and a crushable black bead, polyester melts to a hard bead. Confirm by microscope or solubility test.

Yarn is twisted fibre: staple fibres are short, filament fibres continuous. Twist runs S or Z. Linear density is tex, grams per 1,000 metres.

sections.heading: Fabric construction
sections.text: Woven cloth has warp threads (lengthwise, usually stronger and more twisted) and weft threads. Plain weave crosses one over one; twill gives a diagonal rib, as in denim; satin floats a thread over several others for lustre. Knitted fabric interlocks loops and stretches; nonwoven felt is bonded, not woven.

sections.heading: Dyeing and printing
sections.text:
Dye is applied at fibre, yarn, piece or garment stage. Reactive dyes bond chemically to cotton; vat dyes need a chemical vat and are generally very fast, though indigo on denim fades; acid dyes suit wool and nylon; disperse dyes need high heat for polyester. A mordant is a metal salt that helps dye attach.

Printing puts colour in a pattern: screen, block, resist (batik, tie-dye), discharge and digital inkjet. Example: 2% dye on weight of fibre for 5 kg of cotton is 0.02 × 5,000 g = 100 g.

sections.heading: Pattern, fastness, finishing
sections.text:
A pattern repeat is the distance before the design repeats. In a half-drop repeat, alternate columns drop by half the repeat height: a 20 cm × 25 cm block is placed every 20 cm across, but the full design repeats every 40 cm across, and each alternate column starts 25 ÷ 2 = 12.5 cm lower.

Colour fastness is resistance to light, washing, rubbing and perspiration, graded on grey scales (1 to 5) and, for light, the blue wool scale (1 to 8). Finishing changes handle and performance. Sustainability concerns water, energy and dye effluent; some azo dyes that can release harmful amines are restricted in many countries, and GOTS (Global Organic Textile Standard) certifies organic textiles.

keyPoints: Fibres are natural or manufactured; the burn test is a rough check confirmed by microscope or solubility tests.
Warp and weft build woven cloth; plain, twill and satin differ in how threads interlace.
The dye class must match the fibre: reactive for cotton, acid for wool and nylon, disperse for polyester.
Dye mass = (percentage on weight of fibre ÷ 100) × mass of fibre; 2% owf on 5 kg cotton needs 100 g.
In a half-drop repeat, alternate columns are offset by half the repeat height.
Colour fastness is graded on grey scales (1 to 5) and, for light, the blue wool scale (1 to 8).

en.title: Graphic design studio: visual identity, layout and print production
en.short: Visual identity, poster and packaging layout, print production, proofing and client presentation.

sections.heading: Brief and identity
sections.text:
A client brief states the problem, audience, message, budget and deadline. Ask who the audience is, where they meet the design and what they must do. A bakery needing packaging and a shop sign needs shelf impact and clear opening hours, not one design at both sizes.

Visual identity is a consistent system of logo, colour, type, imagery and tone across applications. A short brand guide records the rules so future users keep the system coherent.

sections.heading: Layout and hierarchy
sections.text:
Layout arranges words and images on a page or pack. Hierarchy is the order in which the eye finds information: usually one dominant message, then supporting detail. A poster read across a room needs fewer, larger elements than a leaflet held in the hand.

A grid is a set of margins, columns and guides that aligns elements and speeds decisions. For packaging, draw a dieline, the flat plan of cut and fold lines, and test a physical mockup before print.

sections.heading: Print basics
sections.text:
Commercial print separates artwork into CMYK: cyan, magenta, yellow and black inks. Spot colour is premixed ink for exact brand colour. Keep logos and text as vector files (line art). Place photographs at about 300 ppi (pixels per inch) at final size; lower pixelates.

Bleed is extra image beyond the trim edge, so cutting leaves no white slivers. A common bleed is 3 mm; follow the printer. An A2 poster (420 × 594 mm) with 3 mm bleed becomes 426 × 600 mm: add 6 mm to each dimension. Crop marks show where to trim.

sections.heading: Proofing and presentation
sections.text:
Proofing checks the job before mass production. A soft proof is viewed on a calibrated screen; a hard proof is a printed sample. Check spelling, colour, images, folds, barcodes and labelling rules. Sign off only when the proof matches the brief.

Present work by explaining how decisions answer the brief: audience, hierarchy, grid and production limits. Show mockups and supply print-ready files and a guide. Invite questions.

keyPoints: A client brief defines audience, message, budget and deadline before design begins.
Visual identity is a consistent system of logo, colour, type, imagery and tone, recorded in brand guidelines.
Hierarchy orders information so the main message is seen first, and a grid aligns elements.
Print artwork usually uses CMYK, with spot colour for exact brand colour and vector files for logos and text.
Place photographs at about 300 ppi at final size, and for 3 mm bleed add 6 mm to width and height.
Check and sign off proofs, then present work by explaining how decisions meet the brief.

en.title: Typography and lettering
en.short: Type anatomy, classification, spacing, hierarchy, legibility, lettering and signage.

sections.heading: Type anatomy
sections.text: Type anatomy names letter parts. The baseline is the line letters sit on. X-height is the height of lowercase letters such as x. Ascenders rise above it, as in b; descenders fall below the baseline, as in p. A counter is enclosed space, as in o. Serifs are small strokes at stroke ends. A typeface is a design; a font is a particular size, weight and style. Classification commonly uses serif, sans serif, slab serif, script and display, though systems differ.

sections.heading: Spacing and setting
sections.text: Spacing controls rhythm. Tracking is overall space between letters in a word or line. Kerning adjusts one pair, such as A and V, so they look evenly spaced. Leading is baseline-to-baseline distance. A 10/12 setting uses 10-point type on 12-point leading; 30 line boxes occupy about 30 × 12 = 360 points, about 127 mm, before paragraph spacing. Tight or loose spacing can hurt reading. Legibility depends on x-height, contrast, line length, alignment and space.

sections.heading: Choosing and hierarchy
sections.text: Type selection starts with purpose, audience, medium and reading distance. Long text needs a readable face; a poster or sign needs quick recognition. Check licensing: some fonts are free, others need a licence. Hierarchy shows what matters first through size, weight, position, colour and white space. Use few levels and keep them consistent. Layout uses a grid, columns, alignment and margins. Good hierarchy guides the eye without confusing it.

sections.heading: Lettering and signage
sections.text: Hand lettering draws letters for a particular use; calligraphy writes them with a broad-edged or pointed pen, brush or other tool, often in a flowing style. Both need practice in stroke order, spacing and rhythm. In signage, legibility at distance is critical. Use strong contrast, simple letterforms, generous spacing and short messages. Check local access and safety standards for letter heights and mounting. Test a sign from the viewing distance and in real light before production.

keyPoints: Type anatomy includes baseline, x-height, ascenders, descenders, counters and serifs.
Typefaces are commonly classified as serif, sans serif, slab serif, script and display, though systems vary.
Tracking spaces a whole word or line, kerning adjusts a single pair, and leading sets baseline-to-baseline distance.
In a 10/12 setting, 30 line boxes occupy about 30 × 12 = 360 points, about 127 mm.
Hierarchy uses size, weight, position, colour and space to show reading order.
Hand lettering and calligraphy need practice, and signage needs distance legibility, contrast and checks against local standards.

en.title: Illustration and visual narrative
en.short: Book, editorial, comics and storyboard illustration: character, sequence, viewpoint, pacing and reproduction.

sections.heading: Illustration as communication
sections.text: Illustration is drawing or image-making made to carry or support a text. Book illustration may decorate a story or explain a fact. Editorial illustration comments on an article, often through metaphor. Comics tell a story in panels, and storyboards plan shots for film, animation or advertising. In each, the image must work with the words, not repeat them. Ask what the reader needs to feel or know, then choose one clear idea.

sections.heading: Character and viewpoint
sections.text: Character design gives a figure a consistent shape, face, costume and posture. A model sheet, which shows the character from several angles, helps others draw it the same way. Viewpoint means where the viewer stands: high angle, low angle, close-up or wide shot. A low angle can make a figure powerful; a high angle can make it small. Choose viewpoint to serve the story moment, not for variety alone.

sections.heading: Sequence and pacing
sections.text: Visual pacing is the control of rhythm across a sequence. In comics, panel size, number per page and gaps guide reading speed. A large panel slows the eye; many small panels speed it up. Storyboards use shot sizes and transitions in the same way. Thumbnails, tiny rough sketches, test the sequence before detail. For a children’s book set in Ibadan, an invented case, the artist might use wide spreads for the journey and a close-up for the lost child’s face.

sections.heading: Roughs to final art
sections.text: Roughs are loose drawings that settle composition, character and sequence. A final artwork is the finished image prepared for reproduction, meaning printing or screen display. For print, keep important detail inside the safe area, allow bleed at the edge, and work at the size and resolution the printer asks for. Present work professionally: clean scans, correct colour, labelled files and a short rationale. A portfolio should show thumbnails, roughs and finals so viewers see how you think.

keyPoints: Illustration supports a text and should add meaning rather than repeat it.
Character design needs consistency, often recorded on a model sheet.
Viewpoint and shot size shape how a reader reads a scene.
Visual pacing controls reading speed through panel size, sequence and gaps.
Roughs test ideas before final artwork; final art must suit its reproduction method.
Present thumbnails, roughs and finals together to show your process.

en.title: Photography studio: camera, light and digital workflow
en.short: Camera controls, exposure, lighting, composition, digital workflow, documentary and studio ethics.

sections.heading: Camera controls and exposure
sections.text: A camera controls exposure, light reaching the sensor, through aperture, shutter speed and ISO. Aperture is the lens opening; a smaller f-number means a wider opening and less depth of field. Shutter speed is how long the sensor is exposed; fast speeds freeze motion. ISO sets sensitivity; higher ISO brightens but adds noise. These three form the exposure triangle. One stop means doubling or halving exposure. Example: f/8, 1/125 second, ISO 100. Each step adds one stop: f/8 to f/5.6, 1/125 to 1/60, or ISO 100 to 200. Check the meter and histogram, not the screen alone.

sections.heading: Light and composition
sections.text: Studio light is shaped with a key light, the main source, and fill light, which softens shadows. A softbox is a large diffuser that makes light softer. Place the key at an angle, control contrast, and use a background light. In documentary work, use available light and watch windows and shade. Composition arranges the frame: decide what to include, use leading lines, balance, and negative space. The rule of thirds is a guide, not a law. Take several frames and check edges and focus.

sections.heading: Digital workflow and selection
sections.text: Workflow is the repeatable path from capture to delivery. Copy files from the card to two drives, keep one off-site. Add file information such as creator, date and place. Select by technical quality and meaning; reject blurred, duplicated or misleading frames. Basic editing adjusts exposure, contrast, colour and cropping. Keep an unedited original. Export a copy at the size and format the use requires. Name files and record versions.

sections.heading: Documentary, studio and ethics
sections.text: Documentary photography records events and people; studio photography builds images under controlled light. Both need consent and care. Photographing people and places raises privacy, dignity and context: explain your purpose, ask before portraits, respect private property and do not expose vulnerable people to harm. Avoid captions that change meaning. Manipulation should be disclosed where it affects truth. Laws and publication rules differ by country; check local law and publisher policy.

keyPoints: Aperture, shutter speed and ISO together set exposure; one stop doubles or halves the exposure effect.
A smaller f-number gives a wider aperture and less depth of field.
Key and fill lights shape studio contrast, and softboxes diffuse light.
Composition decides framing, balance and what the viewer sees; the rule of thirds is only a guide.
A safe workflow copies, backs up, selects, edits a copy and exports with file information.
Photographing people and places requires consent, dignity and honest captions; check local law and publisher policy.

en.title: Digital art and media
en.short: Raster and vector images, digital painting, compositing, animation, output, file and colour management, ethics.

sections.heading: Raster and vector
sections.text: A raster image is a grid of pixels, each pixel being one small square of colour. Its pixel dimensions and its resolution, measured in pixels per inch (ppi), set how much detail it holds. Enlarging a raster image far beyond its pixel count makes it soft or blocky. A vector image stores shapes as mathematical paths, so it scales to any size without losing edge quality. Use raster for photographs and painted texture, and vector for logos, type and diagrams.

sections.heading: Painting and compositing
sections.text: Digital painting uses a pressure-sensitive tablet and software brushes that imitate media. Work on separate layers: a layer is an independent level of the image, so sketch, colour and shading can be changed without spoiling each other. Compositing means combining images, such as a photograph with painted elements, into one picture. Match light direction, colour temperature and edge softness, or the join will show. Keep every source file.

sections.heading: Animation and output
sections.text: Basic animation moves or changes elements over time. Frame-by-frame animation draws each frame; keyframe animation sets positions at chosen moments and lets the software fill the frames between them, called tweening. A common rate for cinema is 24 frames per second, though television and web differ. For screen, export images in sRGB, the standard colour space for screens, at the pixel size the display needs. For print, supply high-resolution files in CMYK, the four printing inks (cyan, magenta, yellow and black), and check the printer’s requirements.

sections.heading: Files, colour, ethics
sections.text: Name files and folders consistently, with dates and version numbers, and back up in two places. Colour management keeps colour predictable: a colour profile describes the range of colours a device can show or print. Convert to the printer’s profile at the end, not at the start. Responsible use means crediting makers, respecting licences and copyright, and getting consent for images of people. Copyright law differs by country; check the local rule.

keyPoints: Raster images are grids of pixels and lose quality when enlarged; vector images are paths and scale freely.
Resolution in ppi links pixel size to printed size.
Layers keep parts of an image separate so each can be edited.
Compositing works when light direction, colour and edges match.
Keyframe animation sets key poses and the software tweens between them.
Colour profiles keep colour predictable; convert to the output profile last.

en.title: Modern and contemporary art history
en.short: Modern and contemporary movements, African modernisms, criticism, institutions and markets.

sections.heading: Modern movements
sections.text: Modernism, from the mid nineteenth century, questioned academic rules and explored new form, medium and subject. Realism pictured daily life; Impressionism studied light and perception; Post-Impressionism pushed colour and structure. Cubism broke objects into facets. Dada attacked art during and after the First World War, and Surrealism explored dream and the unconscious. After 1945, Abstract Expressionism, Pop, Minimalism and Conceptual art debated gesture, mass culture, objects and ideas. The avant-garde means artists who challenge conventions. Postmodernism doubted progress and mixed styles, irony and critique.

sections.heading: African modernisms
sections.text: African modernisms are not copies of Europe. Artists negotiated colonial art schools, nationalism and diaspora. In Nigeria, the Zaria Art Society, formed in 1958 by students including Uche Okeke, Demas Nwoko and Bruce Onobrakpeya, argued for natural synthesis: select from African and Western traditions to make new art. Okeke linked this to Igbo uli design and postcolonial identity. Négritude, a cultural movement founded by Aimé Césaire, Léopold Sédar Senghor and Léon-Gontran Damas, shaped debates about black cultural affirmation. Similar projects appeared in Senegal, Ghana and South Africa through magazines, universities and exhibitions.

sections.heading: Institutions and markets
sections.text: Criticism, museums, galleries, biennales and the art market shape which works are seen and valued. A biennale is a large international exhibition held every two years. Critics write reviews; curators select and interpret works; dealers and auction houses set prices. These institutions can widen access or reinforce a canon, the accepted list of art. Social change enters through patronage, funding, censorship and protest. The 1989 exhibition Magiciens de la Terre in Paris placed artists from Africa, Asia and Oceania beside Western artists, and critics debated whether this was genuine exchange or a centre-periphery framing.

sections.heading: Debates and present
sections.text: Contemporary art since the 1990s is often global, installation-based and socially engaged, but not one style. Debates ask who speaks for whom, how museums acquired collections, and whether markets reward novelty over meaning. Connect each work to criticism, display, funding and audience, not only form.

keyPoints: Modernism questioned academic rules through movements such as Realism, Cubism, Dada and Surrealism.
Postmodernism doubted linear progress and mixed styles, irony and critique.
African modernisms negotiated colonial training, nationalism and diaspora, as in Nigeria’s Zaria Art Society and its idea of natural synthesis.
Critics, curators, museums, biennales and dealers shape which works are seen and valued.
Markets and institutions can widen access or reinforce a canon.
Always link a work to its criticism, display, funding and social context, not only its form.

en.title: Art criticism and curatorship
en.short: Describing, interpreting and evaluating art, plus critique, labels, catalogues and curating.

sections.heading: Criticism and critique
sections.text:
Art criticism is written argument about art. A reliable order is description, analysis, interpretation and evaluation. Description states what is visible: medium, size, subject, colours, marks. Analysis explains how the parts work together. Interpretation proposes meaning using evidence from the work and its context. Evaluation judges quality against stated criteria, such as coherence or effectiveness. Taste is not proof; name the criterion you use.

Studio critique follows the same order. Describe before judging. Ask what the maker intended, then give specific, actionable comments. Saying that a dark shape pulls the eye from the face teaches more than a bare dislike. Separate the work from the person.

sections.heading: Exhibition and display
sections.text:
An exhibition is an argument made with objects and space. The curator researches, selects works, checks condition and conservation needs, plans layout, lighting and sightlines, and writes interpretation. A checklist records each work and its requirements. Display should serve the works and the visitor: sequence, height, space and light matter. Loan, insurance and copyright rules vary by country and institution, so confirm them locally.

Case: Amaka, a student curator at a university gallery in Ibadan, plans five printmakers. She groups works by theme, leaves space between frames, and tests the route with visitors. She writes one label per work and a short wall text explaining the theme.

sections.heading: Labels, catalogue, audience
sections.text:
An object label normally gives artist, title, date, medium, dimensions and credit line. Interpretive text adds context in plain language. Keep labels short, accurate and readable at the intended distance. A catalogue may contain a curator’s essay, entries on works and a checklist. Write from evidence, distinguish fact from interpretation, and avoid unsupported claims.

Audience matters. Ask who the exhibition addresses. Accessibility includes seating, large print, captions and clear language. The curator is a mediator and steward, not merely a selector with taste. The role includes research, care of objects, ethical dealing, interpretation, budgets and teamwork. Curators record decisions and evaluate exhibitions through visitor feedback.

keyPoints: Criticism moves from description and analysis to interpretation and evaluation.
In studio critique, describe before judging and comment on the work, not the person.
An exhibition is an argument shaped by selection, sequence, space, light and interpretation.
Object labels give basic facts; catalogue and wall texts add evidence-based context.
The curator researches, cares for objects, interprets, works with a team and considers the audience.
Rules on loans, insurance and copyright vary by country and institution, so check locally.

en.title: Museum and gallery studies: collections, care and public trust
en.short: Collections, documentation, conservation, display, provenance, ethics and public education in museums and galleries.

sections.heading: Collections and records
sections.text:
Collections management is the routine care and control of a museum’s holdings. It covers acquisition, accessioning, cataloguing, storage, loans and inventory. Accessioning means formally accepting an object and giving it a unique number. A catalogue record notes maker, title, date, materials, dimensions, condition and provenance. Good records make objects findable and help prove lawful title.

Documentation follows the object through time: condition reports, photographs, location changes and treatment notes. Records should be backed up and kept secure.

sections.heading: Provenance and ethics
sections.text:
Provenance is the documented history of ownership and movement of an object. Curators check it before acquisition using due diligence: receipts, export permits and catalogues. The UNESCO 1970 Convention aims to stop illicit import, export and transfer of ownership of cultural property. National laws differ, so check the rules of the countries involved.

Ethics cover conflict of interest and sacred objects. Restitution is the return of cultural property to a source community or country. Claims rest on law, evidence and ethics. A fictional case: Ama, a curator in Accra, is offered a mask without papers. She declines until title is clear.

sections.heading: Conservation and climate
sections.text: Conservation is the care and treatment of objects to slow decay. Preventive conservation controls the environment, handling, storage, pests and light. Temperature and relative humidity should be stable; sudden changes damage wood, paper and textiles. Light fades dyes and pigments, so displays use low light levels and UV filters. In hot, humid climates, mould and insects are major risks; in dry, dusty climates, cracking and abrasion are common. Conservators record every treatment.

sections.heading: Display and education
sections.text:
Display turns research into public interpretation. Labels give maker, date, materials and context in clear language. Mounts, cases, lighting and security protect objects while allowing viewing. Accessibility includes readable text, ramps and varied formats.

Public education includes tours, school programmes, talks, publications and digital access. Galleries can consult communities about how their objects are shown. The aim is trust: visitors should understand what is shown, how it was acquired and why it matters.

keyPoints: Collections management covers acquisition, accessioning, cataloguing, storage, loans and inventory.
Documentation records provenance, condition and location, and supports lawful title.
Due diligence checks provenance and export permits before acquisition; the UNESCO 1970 Convention opposes illicit transfer.
Restitution claims rest on law, evidence and ethics, and views differ.
Preventive conservation controls climate, light, pests and handling; risks vary between humid and dry climates.
Display and public education should interpret objects clearly and build trust with communities.

en.title: Art education and community practice
en.short: Planning and assessing art lessons, studio safety, inclusive teaching, and ethical community projects.

sections.heading: Planning lessons
sections.text: Start from clear learning outcomes: what students should know or be able to do by the end. A lesson plan sequences a short demonstration, guided practice, independent studio time and a closing review. List materials, tools, time and room layout. Plan for mixed abilities with extra support and extension tasks. For example, in a Lagos secondary school, a teacher planning a collage lesson might show one example, give a simple cutting task, then let stronger students add texture. Check the plan against available materials and the school timetable.

sections.heading: Assessment and inclusion
sections.text: Assess against stated criteria, not taste. A rubric names criteria such as use of colour, composition, craft and reflection, and describes levels of performance. Use formative assessment, feedback during work, and summative assessment, a final judgement. Include self and peer review. Inclusive teaching offers more than one way to take part: spoken, written and visual instructions, accessible tools, and respect for different cultural references. Avoid assuming a student’s background or ability.

sections.heading: Studio safety
sections.text: Safety is part of planning. Identify hazards such as dust, solvents, sharp tools, heat and electrical equipment. Provide ventilation, safe storage, labelled containers, washing facilities and suitable protective equipment. Teach procedures before practical work and supervise closely. Check local workplace safety law and your school’s policy, because rules differ by country. Keep a first-aid plan and record incidents.

sections.heading: Community projects
sections.text: Community workshops, murals and participatory projects begin with local needs, not the artist’s idea alone. Meet residents and partners, ask what they want, and agree aims, budget, access and language. Ethical consent means informed, voluntary and ongoing permission, including guardian consent and, for minors, the child’s own agreement (assent). Agree who owns the design, how people are credited, and how images may be used. For a mural, confirm written permission from the wall owner, check the surface and weather, and show the design to the community before painting. Evaluate honestly and leave a maintenance plan.

keyPoints: A lesson plan starts from learning outcomes and sequences demonstration, practice, studio time and review.
Assessment should use clear criteria and a rubric, with formative feedback and summative judgement.
Inclusive teaching gives multiple ways to take part and avoids assumptions about background or ability.
Studio safety requires hazard identification, ventilation, safe storage, protective equipment, supervision and local rules.
Community projects start from local needs and agreed aims, access, language and budget.
Ethical consent is informed, voluntary and ongoing, with guardian consent and child assent for minors, and agreed credit and image use.

en.title: Professional practice for artists and designers
en.short: Covers studio business, pricing, contracts, copyright, commissions, portfolios, grants and exhibition proposals.

sections.heading: Studio business and pricing
sections.text: Treat studio work as a small business. Keep records of income, expenses, materials and time. Separate personal and business money where possible. Pricing should cover materials, studio overhead, your time and a sum for risk and tax. A simple method is cost plus a fee. Example: materials 20,000, studio overhead 5,000, 12 hours at 2,000 = 24,000, total cost 49,000. Add a 20% mark-up: 49,000 × 0.20 = 9,800, so quote 58,800. Check tax rules in your country.

sections.heading: Contracts and copyright
sections.text: A contract is a legally enforceable agreement. For a commission, put in writing: scope, fee, payment stages, deadlines, revisions, expenses, cancellation, credit and who owns or licenses the work. Copyright is the exclusive right to copy, publish and adapt a work. It usually begins with the creator, but it can be licensed or assigned. Rules on duration, exceptions, moral rights (such as attribution) and registration vary by country. Check current national law and take professional advice before signing.

sections.heading: Commissions and portfolios
sections.text: Agree commissions in stages: brief, sketch, approval, production, delivery. Ask for a deposit before starting. Keep the client’s written approval of each stage. A portfolio shows selected work, not everything. Include images, short captions, your role and date. Tailor it to the opportunity. Case: Amina, a Lagos illustrator, signs a book commission. The contract limits revisions to two rounds and licenses print rights for one year. She keeps the original artwork and can license it again after that.

sections.heading: Grants and proposals
sections.text: A grant proposal states the project, why it matters, who benefits, the budget and the timeline. Follow the funder’s rules exactly. An exhibition proposal includes a concept, images, technical needs, space plan and artist statement. Show that the work is ready or achievable. Keep copies of applications and reports. Funding and exhibition rules differ by country and institution, so check current guidelines.

keyPoints: Treat art practice as a small business with clear records and separate money.
A simple quote is materials + overhead + time + mark-up, then check tax rules.
Put every commission in a written contract covering scope, fee, deadlines, revisions, credit and rights.
Copyright usually starts with the creator, but duration, exceptions and moral rights vary by country.
A portfolio should show selected, relevant work with captions and your role.
Grant and exhibition proposals must follow current guidelines and state a realistic budget and timeline.

en.title: Research methods in art and design
en.short: Practice-led research, visual analysis, interviews, archives, case studies, ethics and project writing.

sections.heading: Asking research questions
sections.text: A research question states what you want to find out and why it matters. Write it as a question, not a topic. It should be focused, answerable with the time and materials you have, and connected to existing work. A literature review is a critical survey of published and exhibited sources, not a list. It shows what is known, where authors disagree and what gap your project addresses. Keep a working bibliography from the start.

sections.heading: Methods and evidence
sections.text: Practice-led research treats studio making as a way of generating knowledge, not only as illustration. The work is documented and reflected on, and the written report explains the decisions and discoveries. Visual analysis examines form, subject and context. Interviews can gather makers’ or users’ views; use open questions, record with consent and transcribe carefully. Archives include museum records, photographs, catalogues and oral histories; check provenance (ownership history), access and copyright. A case study examines one bounded example in depth, such as a student project on an adire dyeing cooperative in Abeokuta, Nigeria, using interviews, photographs and documents to compare evidence. Evidence may be primary (your own work, interviews, objects) or secondary (books, articles, catalogues).

sections.heading: Ethics and documentation
sections.text: Ethics covers consent, anonymity, fair payment, safety and respect for cultural knowledge. Ask permission before photographing people or sacred objects, follow local community protocols, and seek institutional ethics approval where required. Documentation means keeping dated notes, sketches, photographs with metadata (date, place, maker), recordings and versions. It lets others check your evidence and protects your work.

sections.heading: Writing the report
sections.text: Academic writing for a project report usually moves from question to method, evidence, analysis and conclusion. Make a claim, support it with evidence, then explain its significance. The report should show how your practice and written evidence answer the question. Cite every source and image, and avoid plagiarism. Edit for clarity.

keyPoints: A research question should be focused, answerable and connected to a gap in existing work.
A literature review critically surveys sources and shows the gap, not just lists them.
Practice-led research uses studio making as inquiry, with documentation and written reflection.
Interviews, archives and case studies need consent, provenance checks and careful documentation.
Ethics includes consent, anonymity, cultural protocols and institutional approval where required.
A project report argues from evidence, cites all sources and images, and avoids plagiarism.

en.title: Final project: studio work and exhibition
en.short: From proposal to exhibition: documentation, artist statement, installation, oral defence and presentation.

sections.heading: Proposal to body
sections.text:
A final studio project begins with a proposal, a short written plan stating your question or idea, media, method, timetable and realistic budget. Check your department’s format and deadlines, because these vary by institution and country. The proposal guides you; record changes in a logbook.

Build a coherent body of work, a group of pieces linked by theme, process or form. Aim for depth, not many unrelated objects. For example, imagine a painting student in Enugu who proposes five works on market light. She reduces the scale and adds two studies after testing costs. Her final body has seven pieces sharing one idea.

sections.heading: Documentation and statement
sections.text:
Document every stage: photographs of work in progress, notes on materials and decisions, and a list of works with title, year, medium and dimensions. Use consistent lighting and a plain background for final images. Keep backups.

An artist statement is a short first-person text explaining what you make, why and how. It should be specific and free of jargon. Write it late, when the work is clear, then ask a tutor to check it. The statement supports the work; it does not replace it.

sections.heading: Installation and presentation
sections.text:
