Exhibition installation is the physical arrangement of works, labels, lighting and space. Make a plan or maquette, a small scale model. Check sight lines, height, security, cables and fire exits. Labels usually give artist, title, year, medium and dimensions. Confirm local rules with your gallery or school.

Professional presentation includes a clean portfolio, a CV, business cards and clearly named digital files. Practise speaking about the work in two minutes and in ten minutes.

sections.heading: Oral defence
sections.text:
An oral defence is a spoken examination where you explain the project and answer questions. Prepare by rehearsing your aims, process, influences and possible changes. Answer honestly; if you do not know, say so and explain how you would find out.

Bring the work, documentation and statement. Arrive early, test equipment and thank the panel.

keyPoints: Start with a proposal that states your idea, media, method, timetable and budget, and check your department’s format.
Build a coherent body of work linked by theme, process or form rather than many unrelated pieces.
Document work in progress and final pieces, and keep backups of images and notes.
An artist statement explains what you make, why and how in clear first-person prose.
Plan installation with a maquette and check labels, lighting, sight lines, security and local rules.
Prepare for oral defence by rehearsing your aims and process, and present a clean portfolio.

en.title: Advanced art theory and aesthetics
en.short: Formalism, expression, institutional theory, postcolonial critique, representation, taste and value.

sections.heading: Formalism and expression
sections.text: Formalism judges art by formal qualities: line, colour, shape and composition rather than subject matter or context. Clive Bell, in Art (1914), called the quality that moves us “significant form”; Roger Fry made similar arguments. Formalism trains close looking, but it can ignore meaning, politics and use. Expression theory says art expresses feeling or intuition. Leo Tolstoy, in What Is Art? (1898), tied art to the communication of feeling; R. G. Collingwood, in The Principles of Art (1938), said art clarifies emotion. Expression is not mere release: a work may express what the artist did not intend, and viewers may disagree.

sections.heading: Institutional and social
sections.text: Institutional theory asks what makes something art. Arthur Danto’s essay “The Artworld” (1964) argued that an artwork needs an interpretive context; George Dickie (1974) described the artworld as a social institution that confers status. This explains how Marcel Duchamp’s Fountain (1917), a signed urinal, could become art, but critics say the theory is circular and says little about quality. Aesthetics also studies taste. David Hume (1757) asked whether a standard of taste exists despite differences in feeling; Immanuel Kant (1790) distinguished a disinterested judgment of beauty (judging the work for its own sake, not for use or reward) from mere charm. Value is plural: aesthetic, social and market value can conflict. Art may affirm power, criticise it, or build community identity.

sections.heading: Representation and critique
sections.text: Representation is how images, signs and stories stand for something. It is never neutral: framing, medium and genre shape what is shown and what is left out. Postcolonial critique examines how colonial power produced images and knowledge about colonised peoples. Edward Said’s Orientalism (1978) is a key study of such representation. Decolonial critique goes further, questioning Eurocentric categories of art and beauty and asking whose standards set value. Scholars disagree about whether universal standards are possible or desirable. A concrete case: a museum that labels a carved mask “artifact” rather than “art” makes a claim about value; relabelling changes institutional status, but it does not restore the carver’s context.

keyPoints: Formalism values formal qualities but can ignore context and meaning.
Expression theory treats art as the communication or clarification of feeling.
Institutional theory explains how the artworld confers art status, but not quality.
Taste is both personal and social; Hume and Kant asked whether judgment can be shared.
Postcolonial and decolonial critique examine how power shapes representation and value.
Artistic value is plural, and art can affirm, criticise or build social identity.

en.title: Research methods for the art dissertation
en.short: Research design, literature review, archives, ethics, documentation and writing for MA and MFA art dissertations.

sections.heading: Designing the study
sections.text: A dissertation answers a question, not just a theme. State one research question narrow enough to finish within your time and resources, then choose methods that fit it: interviews, observation, close reading, archival work, or documented studio trials. An MA thesis is usually text-based. In an MFA practice-led thesis the studio work generates knowledge, and the written component explains the process and its claims; Robin Nelson calls this practice as research. Keep a dated reflective journal from the first week.

sections.heading: Sources and archives
sections.text: The literature review maps what is already known and names the gap you address. Search subject databases, not only search engines, and follow one citation style throughout, such as Harvard, APA or Chicago, as your department requires. Archival research uses primary documents: letters, exhibition catalogues, photographs, colonial-era records. Request material in advance, handle originals carefully, and record box, folder and access date so that others can retrace your steps.

sections.heading: Ethics and consent
sections.text: Most institutions require ethics approval before fieldwork. Informed consent means explaining the purpose, the risks and the right to withdraw, and recording agreement in writing. Anonymise participants if you promised to. For photographs of people, or of community-owned or sacred objects, ask permission and agree the credit. Example: Adaeze, an MFA student in Kumasi, interviews indigo dyers; she promises not to publish recipes that families treat as secret.

sections.heading: Documenting and writing
sections.text: Keep a documentation log recording date, materials, decisions and failures, and photograph work in consistent light. For interview data, coding means labelling passages to find patterns. In the thesis, separate description from interpretation and signpost with short sentences. Cite every borrowed idea. Draft early, revise, and proofread aloud. Examiners look for a clear question, a fair account of sources, honest ethics and evidence that supports each claim.

keyPoints: A dissertation is built around one answerable research question, not a broad theme.
Methods must fit the question; in a practice-led thesis the studio work is evidence, explained in the written component.
The literature review must identify the gap, using a single citation style throughout.
Ethics approval and informed consent come before fieldwork, including for images and community knowledge.
A dated documentation log with consistent photographs makes studio evidence traceable.
Separate description from interpretation, and cite every borrowed idea.

en.title: Contemporary African art, globalisation and restitution
en.short: Globalisation, diaspora, biennales, markets and repatriation in contemporary African art.

sections.heading: Globalisation and decolonisation
sections.text: Contemporary African art usually means work made by artists from Africa and its diaspora since the mid-twentieth century, though periodisation varies. Globalisation is the intensified movement of people, money, images and ideas across borders. It has opened exhibitions, residencies and markets, but it can also force African work into Western categories such as “contemporary” versus “traditional”. Decolonisation here means critiquing Eurocentric canons, museum practice and collecting, not only flag independence. Scholars disagree on whether global visibility widens access or reproduces unequal power.

sections.heading: Diaspora and biennales
sections.text: Diaspora practices are made by artists and audiences living outside the continent, often through transnational identities, memory and hybrid forms. A biennale is a large recurring exhibition, typically held every two years, usually international and theme-led. Dak’Art, the Dakar Biennale, and the Venice Biennale are well-known examples. Biennales create visibility and networks, but they depend on funding, travel and gatekeepers. Curators from Africa and the diaspora have used them to challenge centre-periphery assumptions, though critics warn that international attention can be seasonal and market-driven.

sections.heading: Markets and display
sections.text: The art market has a primary market of galleries and dealers, and a secondary market of auctions. Major fairs and auctions are concentrated in Europe, North America and Asia, while African scenes vary by city and country. The politics of display concerns labels, lighting, chronology and wall texts: who is shown as “contemporary”, who as “traditional”, and who speaks for the work. Collection concerns acquisition, ownership and storage by museums, private collectors and companies. Acquisition policies and catalogues shape what later counts as art history.

sections.heading: Repatriation debates
sections.text: Repatriation, or restitution, means returning cultural objects to source communities or countries. The Benin Bronzes are a central case: in 1897 a British military expedition looted objects from Benin City, in present-day Nigeria. Museums and Nigerian authorities have debated return, long-term loans and shared custody. Arguments appeal to legal title, ethics, universal access and source-community rights. No single rule governs outcomes; agreements differ by country and institution, so check current official statements.

keyPoints: Globalisation increases flows of people, money, images and ideas but can reproduce unequal power in art institutions.
Decolonisation in art means critiquing Eurocentric canons, display and collecting, not only political independence.
Diaspora practices are shaped by transnational identity, memory and hybrid forms.
Biennales such as Dak’Art and Venice create visibility and networks but depend on funding and gatekeepers.
Art markets have primary and secondary sectors, with major auctions and fairs concentrated in the global north.
Repatriation debates concern return, loans and shared custody of looted objects, as with the Benin Bronzes.

en.title: Advanced studio practice and exhibition
en.short: Sustained critique, a coherent body of work, documentation, exhibition planning and public presentation.

sections.heading: The studio seminar
sections.text:
A studio seminar is a recurring meeting where each artist presents work in progress to peers and staff. At master’s level the critique, or crit, is sustained: it examines intent, material choices and how the work reads to others, not whether it is liked. A studio visit is a one-to-one review; a group crit tests the work against many readings.

Bring the work, a statement of intent and two questions you want answered. Record the responses and act on them later. The aim is a self-directed practice that can defend its choices.

sections.heading: A coherent body
sections.text:
A coherent body is a group of works sharing a question, method or visual language, yet each piece must add something. Coherence is not repetition. Write one sentence covering the whole group; a work needing a different sentence may belong in another project.

Documentation means photographing each work to a consistent standard: even light, neutral background, correct colour. Record title, year, medium, dimensions and edition in an inventory.

sections.heading: Exhibition planning
sections.text:
Exhibition planning starts from a curatorial statement, a short text setting out the idea of the show and how the works relate, then a checklist: each work, its size, weight, hanging method and insurance value. Plan the hang on a scale drawing, check lighting and labels, and agree dates, fees and commission with the venue in writing.

Budget example, in an invented currency: gallery hire 150,000; framing 90,000; transport 40,000; printing 20,000; insurance 15,000; opening 25,000. Total 340,000. At 30 per cent commission, a work priced at 100,000 returns 70,000. 340,000 ÷ 70,000 ≈ 4.9, so five sales break even.

sections.heading: Public presentation
sections.text:
Public presentation includes the exhibition, an artist talk, a portfolio and a press or web text. Rehearse the talk: five minutes on the question behind the work, then the works. Keep a record of what visitors and critics say.

After the show, photograph the installation, update the portfolio and write a short critical reflection.

keyPoints: A master’s crit examines intent and how the work reads to others, not personal taste.
A coherent body shares a question or method without simply repeating itself.
Professional documentation records title, year, medium, dimensions and edition, photographed to a consistent standard.
Exhibition planning needs a curatorial statement, a full checklist and written agreement on dates, fees and commission.
In the budget example, costs of 340,000 against 70,000 net per sale need five sales to break even.
The body of work, the documentation and the public presentation are usually assessed together.
